newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico ruling party pulls out stops in rich north.
newsitem.headline: Mexico ruling party pulls out stops in rich north.

text.p: A few months ago, the opposition National Action Party (PAN) looked like a safe bet to win elections in Mexico's mighty industrial engine room -- the northern state of Nuevo Leon.
Its candidate for governor was from the multi-millionaire elite, well-known for his business acumen and for years as a feisty opponent of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

A string of corruption scandals in the state forced the ouster of the PRI's Gov. Socrates Rizzo in 1996 and a disastrous peso crash in 1994 hurt Nuevo Leon, despite its industrial resilience, almost as badly as the rest of Mexico.

But the PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 68 years, has shown a surprising ability to pull back from the brink of disaster in Nuevo Leon and other northern Mexican states. Ten days before the July 6 vote for six state governors, the Chamber of Deputies, a quarter of the Senate and the mayor of Mexico City, polls had the PRI running neck-and-neck with the PAN in the race for governor in northeastern Nuevo Leon.

"The PAN had every chance of winning in Nuevo Leon. How can you explain that from such a huge lead it is now merely level-pegging the PRI? It is almost inexplicable," said Guillermo Colin, a political analyst in the state capital, Monterrey. "Perhaps its candidates are the problem."
Like other analysts, Colin said PAN complacency and blunders had hurt its chances of winning other industrial states along Mexico's northern border with the United States.

In Nuevo Leon, Fernando Canales Clariond, a steel magnate turned politician who reported his net worth as $90 million, is flying the PAN flag. When he began campaigning in February, opinion polls gave him a 20-point lead over his PRI rival, Natividad Gonzalez Paras, but analysts say his campaign has been tarnished by angry outbursts against the ruling party that may have turned off an already apathetic electorate.

"The race has been sullied by negative campaigning and the airing of a lot of dirty laundry," Ramon de la Pena, head of the State Electoral Council, told Reuters. While he refused to point fingers, he noted that the PAN had been fined for issuing a cartoon depicting the PRI as teeth-gnashing rats -- publicity that for a while Canales refused to withdraw.
In response, former Deputy Interior Minister Gonzalez has staged a brash, modern campaign in which he has cast himself, not his party, as the main selling point.

In a speech to promote his platform in the closing stages of his campaign this week, he never mentioned the PRI and its symbol was nowhere to be seen -- evidence he has distanced himself from a party that is unpopular because of local scandals and years of economic mismanagement.
Borrowing from the opposition that has trumpeted the need for a change after six decades of PRI rule, he unabashedly runs his campaign under the slogan "Responsible change."
"It's a race of candidates, not parties," a Gonzalez aide, who requested anonymity, admitted to Reuters. "Natividad is a good product with a bad brand name."
Whether his tactics will work and voters will pardon the PRI's shortcomings remained to be seen.

Canales, meanwhile, made a last-ditch effort to bring out the vote from some of the army of poor citizens who could swing the results. In his state-of-the-art campaign bus, he pulled into a poor Monterrey neighbourhood this week and played bingo with residents, using pebbles from the road as chips.
"If the PAN loses, there will be war here in Monterrey," said Josefina Ponce de Martinez, a mother of six. "For too long the PRI has gotten rich on the backs of the poor."
